q: A team hard-codes a per-request token budget of 3,000 tokens for a summarization prompt, calibrated by counting tokens on one model during development. Six months later they migrate the same prompt template to a newer model generation with an updated tokenizer, without re-measuring anything, and the pipeline starts truncating input that used to fit comfortably. Which practice would have prevented this?
o: Increase max_tokens instead of re-counting, since max_tokens and input token budgets are governed by the same underlying tokenizer figure.
Re-run token counting against the new model after any migration, since token counts are model-specific and a count calibrated on one model's tokenizer does not reliably transfer to another.
Switch to counting words instead of tokens, since word counts are consistent across all model generations and avoid the tokenizer dependency entirely.
Nothing could have prevented this: token budgets calibrated on one model are guaranteed to transfer exactly to any newer model in the same family.
e: Correct answer B: token counts depend on the specific tokenizer a model version uses, so a budget measured against one model's tokenizer is not safe to reuse unmeasured after a migration; re-counting against the new model is what prevents the silent truncation. Option A confuses two different limits: max_tokens governs output length, not the input token budget being described, so raising it does not address the input-side miscount. Option C is wrong because the token-to-word ratio itself varies by content type and by tokenizer, so word counts are not a stable substitute. Option D asserts a guarantee that directly contradicts the scenario, which demonstrates the opposite.

q: An MCP server for a legal-document workflow exposes a saved instruction such as "Summarize this contract's indemnification clauses," which users pick from a menu inside the Claude application rather than the model deciding to run it on its own. Which primitive does this capability map to?
o: A tool, because it performs an action within the document workflow
A prompt, a user-controlled reusable template invoked explicitly rather than by model decision
A resource, since it packages reference content for the model to read
A sampling request, since the server is asking the client to generate a completion
e: Prompts are the user-controlled primitive: reusable templates a user explicitly selects, never triggered automatically. Tools are model-controlled actions the LLM invokes on its own judgment, which doesn't match a capability chosen from a menu. Resources are application-controlled read-only data pulled into context, not something a user runs. Sampling is a separate MCP mechanism where the server asks the client's model to complete something, unrelated to user-selected templates.

q: A compliance workflow synthesizes conflicting clauses across long contracts using Claude Sonnet 5 at effort high, and the evals gating this workflow were all tuned against that configuration. Latency is now a concern, so an engineer proposes switching the workflow to Claude Haiku 4.5 at effort low to speed things up while keeping quality about the same. What is wrong with this proposal?
o: Nothing is wrong — Haiku 4.5 at effort low will reliably match Sonnet 5's quality on this task
Claude Haiku 4.5 has no effort parameter, and swapping tiers invalidates the evals that were tuned on Sonnet 5's behavior
Effort low always increases latency compared to effort high, so the proposal will make the workflow slower
Claude Sonnet 5 does not support adaptive thinking, so the current baseline is already misconfigured
e: Haiku 4.5 is differently shaped, not just cheaper: it runs extended thinking only and has no effort parameter at all, so 'effort low' on Haiku isn't a valid configuration to begin with. Even setting that aside, a tier swap invalidates every eval run against the old model, which is exactly what the workflow's evals were tuned on — the correct move is to step effort down on Sonnet 5 first, not swap tiers. Option A ignores both problems. Option C inverts the actual relationship between effort and latency (lower effort reduces reasoning depth and typically latency, it doesn't guarantee the opposite outcome described). Option D is a false factual claim — Sonnet 5 does support adaptive thinking.

q: A data pipeline calls Claude to extract structured fields from support tickets, and the extracted JSON is inserted directly into a downstream Postgres table without any application-level validation. The team currently prompts Claude with 'respond only with JSON matching this schema.' Occasionally a field's type mismatches the column type and the insert fails. Which change most directly prevents malformed JSON from being emitted in the first place?
o: Add a stricter instruction telling Claude to double-check its output before responding
Set output_config.format to a json_schema definition matching the required fields and types
Wrap the insert statement in a try/except block and log failures for manual review
Increase max_tokens so the response is never truncated mid-object
e: output_config.format with a json_schema type uses grammar-constrained decoding, so every generated token is restricted to stay inside the schema — malformed JSON and type mismatches become structurally impossible, not just less likely. A prompt instruction is a soft request the model can still violate. Wrapping the insert in try/except only catches the failure after it happens, it does not prevent the malformed output. Raising max_tokens addresses truncation, not field-type mismatches, which is a different failure mode.

q: A backend service calls an internal REST endpoint to create a customer record, and its client library automatically retries any non-2xx response by resubmitting the same request body. During a traffic spike the endpoint starts returning 409 responses, because an earlier request actually succeeded server-side but its response timed out on the client before arriving, so the client never learned it had already succeeded. What is the correct fix?
o: Increase the client's retry count so the 409 eventually succeeds
Treat 409 as equivalent to 429 and apply the same exponential backoff strategy
Have the client check whether the record already exists before resubmitting the create request, rather than blindly retrying with the same body
Switch the endpoint from REST to GraphQL to avoid status-code ambiguity
e: 409 Conflict means the resource already exists in a state that conflicts with the request; the fix is to inspect current state before acting, not to resend the identical request. Increasing retries just repeats the same failure forever, since the conflict never resolves itself. 429 is a rate-limit signal where backoff helps; 409 is a state-conflict signal where backoff does nothing, so treating them the same is a category error. Swapping protocols doesn't touch the actual bug, which is a missing idempotency check.

q: A nightly reconciliation script kicks off at 1 AM and immediately submits all 900 of the day's transaction records to Claude for anomaly review at once, using asyncio.gather with no concurrency cap. Within the first thirty seconds most requests fail with 429 responses, and the on-call engineer's instinct is to just add a longer fixed delay before each retry. What is the more durable fix?
o: Bound concurrency with a semaphore or queue and ramp the request rate up gradually instead of firing all 900 at once
Keep the current fan-out pattern but add a longer fixed delay before each retry
Switch the reconciliation job to a larger, higher-throughput model so more requests succeed per second
Disable the SDK's built-in retry behavior so failed requests fail fast instead of queuing
e: The root cause is unbounded fan-out, not slow retries — bounding concurrency and ramping traffic gradually is what actually keeps the request rate under the limit. A longer fixed delay treats the symptom on each failed call but the next batch still fires all 900 at once and trips the same limit. Model tier does not change organization-level rate limits, so a larger model doesn't help. Disabling the SDK's own retry/backoff removes a mechanism that was already helping and makes the failure mode worse, not better.

q: A platform team's incident postmortem shows that during a partial Claude API outage, request volume to the API nearly tripled because a wrapper library retried every failed call five times with a fixed one-second delay on top of the official SDK client used underneath it. The wrapper also kept retrying 400 responses caused by a recently introduced malformed-request bug, which never succeeded no matter how many attempts were made. Select the two changes the team should make.
o: Remove the custom wrapper's retry loop and rely on the SDK's built-in max_retries and backoff, which already honors retry-after
Increase the SDK's own max_retries from its default of 2 to a much higher number, in addition to keeping the wrapper
Stop retrying 400-class responses, since they indicate a malformed request that will not succeed regardless of attempts
Add a circuit breaker that halts all traffic to the API for 24 hours after any single failure
e: Removing the redundant wrapper eliminates the double-retry layer that multiplied load during the outage, and the SDK's own max_retries/backoff already honors retry-after. Not retrying 400s is correct because that status is a client error the SDK never retries by default — resending a malformed request cannot succeed. Raising max_retries while keeping the wrapper in place makes the storm worse, since both layers now retry harder. A blanket 24-hour halt is wildly disproportionate to a partial outage and one malformed-request bug, and would take down unrelated, healthy traffic.

q: A senior engineer sees that a teammate's pull request, written entirely by Claude Code, passed the project's automated eval suite and every unit test on the first run. The reviewer is ready to approve it with only a skim, reasoning that a model whose own output already validated cleanly is unlikely to have introduced a subtle bug worth digging for. What should the reviewer do instead?
o: Approve with a skim, since passing evals and unit tests is sufficient signal for AI-authored changes
Apply the same review rigor used for human-written code, regardless of who or what authored it
Ask the same model to regenerate the code a second time and diff the two outputs before deciding
Skip review entirely and rely on the CI pipeline as the sole gate for AI-authored pull requests
e: Provenance doesn't change risk: AI-generated code needs the same review rigor as human-written code, because passing tests and evals only proves the code satisfies what was already checked, not that it's free of subtler issues. Approving on a skim (or skipping review entirely) relaxes the control specifically because of authorship, which is the trap. Regenerating and diffing two outputs from the same model is a superficial consistency check — both generations can share the same blind spot, so it doesn't substitute for actual review.

q: A team's Claude-powered ticket-triage prompt has been hand-edited nine times over two months, each time to fix one specific misclassification, but engineers just paste new wording into the console each time rather than committing it anywhere. When the tenth edit reintroduces a bug that edit six had already fixed, nobody can find what changed between them or why. Which practice addresses the root cause?
o: Increase the prompt's temperature so classification becomes more consistent across edits
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt so the model needs fewer manual edits over time
Switch to a larger model that is less prone to misclassification
Treat the prompt as a versioned artifact — commit each revision to the repository and review changes like code
e: The root cause is that prompt revisions were never checked into source control, so nothing could be diffed, reviewed, or bisected when a regression reappeared. Committing and reviewing prompt changes like code is what makes a reintroduced bug findable and preventable. Temperature, few-shot examples, and a larger model are all prompt-tuning moves that leave the missing versioning process untouched, so the same silent regression can recur regardless of which one is applied.

q: A three-line change to a repository's settings.json disables a permission rule that had been blocking a Claude Code agent from running shell commands as root, and it gets merged straight to main because 'it's just a config tweak, not real code.' Two weeks later the same agent runs an unreviewed destructive command in a teammate's branch. Which practice would most directly have prevented this outcome?
o: Require CLAUDE.md and settings.json changes to go through the same pull-request review and CI gates as source code, since they govern what the system is allowed to do
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent never to run destructive commands
Rotate the API key used by the agent on a monthly schedule
Move the permission setting into a code comment inside CLAUDE.md instead of settings.json
e: settings.json and CLAUDE.md are versioned configuration artifacts that determine what the system is allowed to do, and gating them through the same review and CI pipeline as source code is what would have caught the permission change before merge. A system-prompt instruction is a request the agent can still fail to follow; a permission rule is the deterministic control the prompt instruction can't replace. Key rotation is a credential-hygiene practice unrelated to a permission bypass. Moving the setting into a comment removes its enforcement entirely, making the problem worse.

q: A team asks Claude Code to migrate a 40,000-line billing module from a deprecated ORM to its replacement. Partway through, the agent proposes finishing the whole migration in one sweeping commit that also fixes several unrelated bugs it noticed along the way, reasoning that touching each file only once saves review time. The team is under a hard deadline and finds the one-pass approach tempting. What should they require instead?
o: Approve the single large commit, since touching each file only once reduces total review overhead
Let the agent proceed as proposed, but add a longer QA cycle at the very end to catch any issues
Split the migration into bounded increments with tests passing between each step, and keep the unrelated bug fixes in separate changes
Postpone the migration until after the deadline, since large-scale refactors are inherently too risky to attempt under time pressure
e: The correct discipline for large-scale refactoring is bounded increments with tests green between each step, and never mixing a refactor with a behavior change in the same commit — the unrelated bug fixes are behavior changes and must be split out. Approving the single sweep trades safety for review convenience and mixes concerns. Deferring all verification to one QA pass at the end loses the between-step safety net, making any failure hard to attribute to a specific change. Large-scale refactoring is explicitly in scope and doable under deadline pressure; the fix is incremental discipline, not avoidance.

q: A team wants a repeatable way to describe how they take a Claude-powered feature from initial concept through iterative development, release, and ongoing operation. A vendor pitches a proprietary 'AI Development Lifecycle' framework built specifically for LLM-based projects, arguing that generic IT frameworks predate large language models and can't account for non-deterministic behavior.
o: Adopt the vendor's proprietary AI Development Lifecycle, since generic IT frameworks predate LLM applications
Rely on prompt engineering best practices alone, since they govern how the feature behaves in production
Apply the generic systems life cycle (plan, develop, test, implement, operate, maintain) using Agile or DevOps practices, adding evals as the test gate
Design a new lifecycle framework from scratch, since no existing framework accounts for non-deterministic model output
e: The objective is scoped as generic IT systems life cycle management; Claude-application work maps onto the same plan-develop-test-implement-operate-maintain arc as any other system, with Agile or DevOps supplying the iteration and release discipline and evals replacing exact-match tests as the quality gate. Adopting a proprietary 'AI-specific' framework is the trap this objective is built to catch — an engineered-to-sound-plausible distractor that ignores that the generic model already covers this arc. Prompt engineering is a technique applied during development, not a lifecycle framework in its own right. Building a new framework from scratch overstates the problem: non-determinism is handled by changing what the existing test gate checks, not by discarding the gate.

q: A Claude-powered pipeline is already live in production. An engineer wants to bump the pinned model version and adjust two prompts. Company policy requires a documented change record, a risk assessment, and sign-off from a change advisory board before any modification reaches production, regardless of how small the change is. Which management discipline governs this requirement?
o: Scrum sprint planning, since the change can be scoped and sized as a backlog item
Waterfall requirements sign-off, since the system's original scope must be honored
DevOps continuous deployment, which is designed to automate this kind of approval away
ITIL-style change and release management
e: Documented change records, risk assessment, and change advisory board sign-off before any production modification, no matter how small, is the definition of ITIL-style service management governing a live system. Sprint planning organizes how development work gets scheduled and estimated, not how a change to a live production system gets approved. Waterfall governs how a project's own phases are sequenced during initial build, not ongoing change control after go-live. DevOps automates delivery pipelines, but 'automates approval away' directly contradicts the stem's explicit requirement for a human sign-off — a distractor that sounds efficient while ignoring the stated constraint.

q: A team is building an internal tool in a language with no official Anthropic SDK, so they call the Messages API directly over HTTPS. Midway through planning, someone notes that network calls occasionally time out under load and the client must recover without surfacing an error to the user. What have they taken on that the SDK would have handled for them?
o: Nothing — raw HTTP calls behave identically to SDK calls in every respect
Retry-with-backoff logic, SSE event parsing, and typed response handling
A different pricing tier reserved for raw REST access
A separate authentication scheme required only for non-SDK clients
e: Correct: the SDKs wrap the same REST API but add retries with backoff, SSE assembly, and typed models — none of that exists over raw HTTP unless you build it. (A) is wrong because raw HTTP and SDK calls hit the identical endpoint but the SDK adds real behavior on top; they are not equivalent. (C) is wrong because pricing is per-token and identical regardless of transport. (D) is wrong because authentication (the API key) is unchanged whether you use an SDK or call REST directly.

q: An engineering standard states that every outbound Messages API call must automatically retry connection errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff, and that no individual engineer should have to remember to add this per call. Where should this guarantee live?
o: In a README instructing engineers to wrap each call in a try/except that retries manually
In code review comments reminding authors to add retry logic before merging
In the SDK client's default retry configuration, so the guarantee applies regardless of whether an individual engineer remembers to add it
In the system prompt, telling Claude to ask the caller to retry failed requests
e: Correct: 'must happen every time, with no engineer having to remember' describes a deterministic default, and the SDK client's built-in retry configuration (2 retries, exponential backoff, applied automatically) is exactly that. (A) and (B) are both documentation or process — they rely on humans remembering, which is precisely what the requirement rules out. (D) is a category error: a system prompt shapes Claude's generated text, it has no mechanism to intercept or retry a failed HTTP request the client already made.

q: A support engineer is troubleshooting a chat app where the context window fills up mid-conversation, forcing older turns to be dropped. Separately, the app needs to display Claude's reply token-by-token as it's generated. Which mechanism does the Claude API itself use to deliver those tokens to the caller?
o: A persistent WebSocket connection opened by the SDK to api.anthropic.com
Long polling, with the client re-requesting the endpoint every 500ms
A gRPC bidirectional stream negotiated during authentication
Server-Sent Events (SSE), one-way from the API to the caller
e: Correct: the context-window detail is scenery — the actual question is which transport delivers streamed tokens, and the Messages API only ever streams over SSE, one-way server to client. (A) is the classic bait: 'streaming' primes people toward websockets, but Anthropic hosts no websocket endpoint. (B) and (C) are real transports elsewhere in software but neither is what `stream: true` actually uses on this API.

q: A voice assistant streams Claude's reply to a user, who can speak over it to interrupt before it finishes. The interrupt has to reach the application within milliseconds, and the application's connection to Claude for that turn is already an in-flight SSE stream. What should the client-to-application leg use to carry that interrupt?
o: A WebSocket between the browser and the application's own backend, separate from the backend's SSE connection to Claude
Nothing extra — the existing SSE connection to Claude already accepts client-sent interrupts
A second REST POST to a dedicated /messages/interrupt endpoint
Increasing max_tokens so the response finishes before the user can interrupt
e: Correct: SSE is one-way, so a low-latency, bidirectional interrupt channel has to be something the application adds itself — a websocket between browser and backend, sitting alongside (not replacing) the backend's SSE leg to Claude. (B) is wrong because SSE cannot carry client-to-server messages at all. (C) is invented — no such endpoint exists, and even if it did, request/response round-trips add latency the millisecond requirement rules out. (D) doesn't address the interrupt requirement; it just makes the response longer.

q: A team calls the Messages API with raw HTTP instead of an official SDK, citing a need for tight control over the transport layer. Select the two responsibilities this decision requires them to implement themselves that the SDKs provide by default.
o: Retry-with-backoff on transient errors (connection failures, 429, and 5xx responses)
Assembling streamed Server-Sent Events into a usable response object
A lower per-token price, since raw HTTP skips the SDK's markup
API key generation, since raw HTTP requires a different credential type
e: Correct: retries-with-backoff and SSE-to-object assembly are both SDK conveniences the team now has to hand-roll. (C) is wrong because there is no SDK markup — pricing is per-token and set by the API regardless of client. (D) is wrong because the same API key and header-based auth work identically for SDK and raw HTTP calls; nothing about the credential type changes.

q: During a traffic spike, a client starts receiving 429 responses and the team debates how to handle it. Which part of that debate is actually decided by SDK and websocket mechanics — this objective — rather than by rate-limit or token-budget reasoning tested elsewhere?
o: The exact backoff curve to use once a 429 is received
How many tokens per minute the account's rate limit allows
Whether the SDK's default retry configuration already retries 429s automatically, versus a raw HTTP call needing that logic written by hand
Whether truncating conversation history would reduce the 429 rate
e: Correct: 'does the SDK already handle this, or do I have to write it myself for a raw HTTP call' is exactly the SDK-vs-REST mechanics this objective covers. (A) is backoff-curve tuning and (B) is rate-limit capacity planning — both real questions, but they live in Applications & Integration / LLM Fundamentals, not here. (D) is a token-budget mitigation strategy, also outside this objective's narrow scope.

q: A script needs to enumerate every message batch a workspace has ever created, not just the first page the API returns. The team notes that new batches are created daily, so any script hardcoding a fixed number of pages would eventually start missing recent ones. What should the script use?
o: A fixed loop that calls the list endpoint exactly 10 times and stops
The SDK's auto-pagination iterator (for example, `for batch in client.messages.batches.list()`), which fetches additional pages as needed
Raising max_tokens so more batches fit into a single page
Polling a WebSocket endpoint for newly created batches
e: Correct: the buried constraint is that the batch count keeps growing, so a hardcoded page count is exactly the failure mode the SDK's auto-pagination avoids by following cursors until the list is exhausted. (A) is the failure mode itself — a fixed page count. (C) is a category error: max_tokens governs response length for a message generation, not how many list items a page returns. (D) invents a websocket feature the batches-list endpoint doesn't have; listing is a paginated REST endpoint, not a streamed one.

q: A telehealth company routes post-visit session summaries through Claude for clinician review. A newly passed data protection law in the patient's home country prohibits any processing of health data outside that country's borders, even momentarily in transit. Which infrastructure requirement should the solution architecture satisfy?
o: Encrypt the session summary with a customer-managed key before it leaves the clinic's network
Route the request through a regional API endpoint that guarantees in-country processing
Shorten the retention window on stored session summaries to reduce exposure
Increase the request timeout budget to accommodate cross-border network latency
e: The constraint is where processing happens, not how long data is kept or how fast a response arrives. A regional endpoint pins inference to the required jurisdiction. Encryption protects confidentiality in transit but doesn't control the country in which the model actually runs, so it fails the residency requirement outright. Shortening retention addresses how long data is stored, a different requirement dimension than where it's processed. Increasing the timeout is a latency parameter with no bearing on jurisdiction.

q: A brokerage firm's policy states that every response Claude sends to a retail customer must have account numbers stripped before delivery, with no exceptions permitted under any circumstance. A junior engineer proposes solving this by adding a instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to redact account numbers whenever it sees one. What does this requirement actually call for?
o: A longer, more detailed system prompt describing exactly what an account number looks like
A higher reasoning-effort configuration on the model to improve redaction accuracy
Periodic manual audits of a sample of outgoing customer responses
A deterministic post-processing filter that runs on every response before delivery, independent of model behavior
e: "No exceptions permitted under any circumstance" means the requirement demands a guarantee, and a guarantee requires a deterministic control that runs regardless of what the model decides. A prompt instruction, however detailed, is still a request the model tries to follow, not a guarantee, so option 0 fails on the same grounds as the junior engineer's original proposal. Higher reasoning effort can reduce error rates but never eliminates them, so it can't satisfy "no exceptions." Sampled manual audits catch problems after some have already reached customers, which directly contradicts a zero-exception requirement.

q: A project brief for an HR tool reads: 'Claude should draft a personalized onboarding email for each new hire based on their role and start date.' The same brief adds that the tool must stay responsive with sub-second turnaround even when 200 new hires start on the same day. A requirements analyst is sorting these two statements into a functional requirements document and an infrastructure requirements document.
o: Both statements belong in infrastructure requirements, since they both describe system behavior under real operating conditions
Both statements belong in functional requirements, since neither one names a specific vendor or region
The email-drafting behavior is functional; the sub-second-at-200-concurrent-hires statement is infrastructure
The latency statement is functional, since it directly shapes what the end user experiences
e: Functional requirements describe what the system does (draft a personalized email); infrastructure requirements describe the non-functional envelope it must operate within (a throughput and latency constraint under concurrent load). Calling both statements infrastructure ignores that drafting the email is itself the capability being built, not a constraint on it. Calling both functional, on the reasoning that neither names a vendor or region, misses that a capacity/performance ceiling is the textbook definition of an infrastructure requirement regardless of vendor mention. Labeling the latency statement functional conflates user-experienced quality with the feature itself — latency-under-load is a quality attribute, not a capability.

q: A support-ticket pipeline classifies each incoming ticket into billing, technical, or account-access, then hands it to a category-specific prompt tuned for that ticket type. Every ticket follows this same two-step flow, though the specialized prompt used in step two differs meaningfully depending on the category. Which architecture fits this pipeline?
o: A single fixed prompt chain that runs the same two prompts on every ticket regardless of category
Routing: classify the ticket, then dispatch it to the prompt built for that category
An autonomous agent that decides at runtime how many classification passes to run
An orchestrator-workers design where a central call invents ticket categories on the fly
e: Routing fits because the categories are fixed but genuinely need different downstream handling -- that's the definition of routing, not plain chaining. Option A ignores the stated per-category difference in step two, collapsing routing into a single fixed chain. Option C adds agent-level runtime flexibility a fixed two-step flow never needs. Option D misapplies orchestrator-workers, which decides subtasks at runtime -- here the three categories are already known in advance.

q: An engineering-metrics agent must read a 200,000-line CI log to isolate the root cause of a flaky test, then hand a two-paragraph summary back to the parent conversation. The team wants to guarantee the parent's context never fills up with raw log lines, no matter how long the log-scanning takes. Which choice best satisfies that guarantee?
o: Increase the parent's context window so it can hold the entire log alongside the rest of the conversation
Enable prompt caching on the log content so repeated reads are cheaper
Run the log-scanning in a subagent with its own context window and return only the distilled summary
Run the log-scanning in a subagent so it can execute in parallel with the rest of the pipeline
e: A subagent with its own window keeps the raw log isolated; only the condensed summary re-enters the parent's context, which is the guarantee the team wants. A bigger window still fills up with raw lines eventually and doesn't prevent pollution. Prompt caching is a cost/latency optimization -- cached content still occupies context, it doesn't isolate it. Framing the subagent's value as parallel execution names the secondary benefit, not the primary reason, and there's nothing else described running concurrently for it to parallelize against.

q: A team is weighing whether to add a manager agent that delegates a task to three specialist subagents, when a single call already handles that task adequately today. Select the two costs this hierarchy specifically introduces that the single-call design does not have.
o: Additional token cost and latency at every manager-to-worker hop
Errors a worker makes can propagate upward and compound through the manager's synthesis step
The system permanently loses the ability to call external tools
The model's underlying context-window limit becomes smaller than before
e: Hop cost/latency and compounding worker error are the two costs a manager/subagent hierarchy actually adds over a single call. Losing tool-calling ability is false -- hierarchy depth doesn't affect tool access. A shrinking context-window limit is also false -- that's a fixed model property, untouched by how many subagents sit underneath a manager. Both wrong options borrow real-sounding constraints from elsewhere that don't actually apply here.

q: A code-review pipeline must run three checks in the exact same order on every single pull request with no exceptions: lint, then type-check, then test. Which implementation actually guarantees that ordering holds every time?
o: A system prompt instructing an agent to always run lint, type-check, then test in that order
An evaluator-optimizer loop that keeps retrying the three checks until all of them pass
A manager agent that decides at runtime which of the three checks are relevant to run
Fixed code that calls lint, then type-check, then test, with no model in the decision path
e: Only code with no model in the decision path guarantees the order, which is what 'must ... with no exceptions' demands. A system-prompt instruction is a request the model can fail to follow, not a guarantee. An evaluator-optimizer loop assumes criteria to iteratively refine against, which doesn't apply to a fixed three-step checklist, and retries don't guarantee ordering either. A manager deciding which checks are relevant introduces exactly the runtime variability the requirement rules out.

q: A document-tagging task applies the exact same three tags via the same three tools to every document, with no variation across runs. A colleague argues for building this as an autonomous agent instead of a fixed workflow because, in their words, agents are 'more flexible and more modern.' What is the strongest architectural counterargument?
o: Flexibility has no payoff when the steps and tools are already fully known and identical every run; a fixed workflow gets the same result with less cost and less unpredictable behavior
Agents are structurally incapable of reliable tool use, so a workflow is the only option that works at all
Only a workflow can use the Claude API's tool-use feature; agents cannot register tools
An agent architecture always requires a manager delegating to a subagent hierarchy, which this simple task doesn't justify
e: The correct counterargument is a cost/complexity one: identical, fully-known steps get no benefit from agent flexibility, so the workflow wins on cost and predictability. The other three options invent false technical limitations -- agents can call tools reliably, both workflows and agents use the same tool-use feature, and a single agent never requires a manager/subagent hierarchy. Each sounds like a plausible technical fact but fails on that basis alone.

q: A deployment agent must never make more than fifty tool calls in a single run, regardless of how capable the underlying model is or how the prompt is worded, because a runaway run has already caused a production incident. Which control actually guarantees that ceiling holds?
o: A harness-level counter that stops the loop once fifty tool calls have been made, independent of the model's own judgment
Switching to a more capable model that is less likely to get stuck in a loop
Lowering the sampling temperature so the model's tool choices are more consistent
Adding a system-prompt instruction telling the model to stop after fifty tool calls
e: Only a harness-level counter enforced in code guarantees the ceiling, because it doesn't depend on the model choosing to comply. A more capable model reduces how often loops happen but never guarantees a hard limit. Lowering temperature changes variability, not termination. A system-prompt instruction is a request the model can fail to follow, not a guarantee -- the same distinction that makes unbounded loops a harness failure rather than a model failure.

q: A long-running research agent writes short notes to a local file as it works through a forty-step investigation, and reads those notes back on later steps, even though this costs it extra tool calls it wouldn't otherwise need. What best explains why this design choice is worth that overhead?
o: It permanently increases the size of the agent's underlying context window
It gives the agent persistent memory outside the context window, preserving progress and dependencies without keeping the full history in-context
It replaces the harness's responsibility to bound the loop with a timeout or iteration limit
It lets the underlying API retain state between two otherwise unrelated conversations
e: Structured note-taking is a memory pattern: it persists progress and dependencies outside the context window at low overhead, so the agent doesn't need to keep everything in-context. It does not change context-window size, does not substitute for loop-termination bounds, and does not make the API stateful -- each wrong option borrows a real mechanism from an adjacent concern that note-taking doesn't actually touch.

q: An agent's conversation has grown large enough that old tool outputs are consuming most of the available context, even though the agent no longer needs to re-inspect any of them. The team wants the lightest-touch fix available and specifically wants to avoid summarizing anything. Which lever fits?
o: Compaction: summarize the whole conversation and reinitiate a new context window
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the old outputs simply fit
Tool-result clearing: drop the stale raw tool outputs from the message history
Rewrite the system prompt to be shorter
e: Tool-result clearing is the lightest-touch lever and involves no summarization -- it just drops stale raw outputs the agent no longer needs. Compaction is exactly the summarization the team said to avoid. A larger context window doesn't manage anything, it just delays the same growth problem. The system prompt isn't what's consuming context in this scenario, so shortening it doesn't address the stated cause.

q: A Python team wants every tool call and model response validated against typed schemas at development time, with as little custom parsing code as possible, and they explicitly do not need a general-purpose graph engine for branching, cyclical control flow. Which framework fits best?
o: LangGraph, for its explicit graph of nodes and edges
Strands Agents, for its minimal-scaffolding model-driven loop
A hand-rolled loop with no framework at all
PydanticAI, for its typed, validated structured output built on Pydantic models
e: PydanticAI's core value is typed, validated structured output via Pydantic models, which is exactly the team's stated requirement. LangGraph is built around explicit graph orchestration for branching, stateful control flow -- the team explicitly said they don't need that. Strands centers on a thin, model-driven loop, not on schema validation. A hand-rolled loop maximizes the custom parsing and validation code the team wants to minimize, the opposite of what they asked for.

q: A document-review assistant reads legal contracts uploaded by outside counsel and drafts summaries for the internal legal team. The company cannot control how outside counsel formats these documents before upload, and one uploaded contract contains a paragraph formatted to look like a system instruction telling the assistant to also send a copy to an external address. The team wants to keep processing contracts from any outside counsel without manual pre-screening of every upload.
o: Switch the assistant to a larger, more capable model so it better recognizes manipulation attempts
Deliver the uploaded contract text only inside tool_result content, and give the assistant no email-sending tool at all
Increase the sampling temperature so responses are less predictable to an attacker
Add a line to the system prompt asking the model to ignore instructions embedded in uploaded documents
e: The correct fix combines content isolation (the untrusted document text stays in tool_result, distinguishable from real instructions) with least-privilege tooling: with no email-sending capability, an injected instruction to email a copy has nowhere to go, regardless of whether the model complies with it. A larger model is a trap distractor — better instruction-following can make a model more susceptible to embedded injected instructions, not less. Temperature has no bearing on whether embedded instructions are followed. A system-prompt request not to follow embedded instructions is advisory only; it is not an enforced control and can be talked around by a sufficiently crafted injection.

q: A finance-ops agent has a tool that transfers funds between internal accounts. Leadership requires that this tool must never execute without a second human's explicit sign-off, with no exceptions, even if the request comes from an admin user or someone later edits the system prompt. An engineer proposes adding a bold instruction to the system prompt: "ALWAYS require human approval before calling transfer_funds."
o: The bold system-prompt instruction, since Claude reliably follows explicit capitalized directives
A one-time reminder appended to the first user message of each session
A deterministic approval gate in the tool-execution harness that blocks the transfer_funds call from completing until a second human explicitly confirms it
A note in the tool's description field stating that approval is required
e: "No exceptions" is a guarantee, and only code the harness enforces can provide one — text the model reads, no matter how it's phrased or where it's placed, remains a request the model could fail to follow, be argued out of, or simply misjudge. A deterministic gate in the harness can refuse to execute the transfer regardless of what the model outputs. The bold system-prompt line, a session reminder, and a tool-description note are all variations on the same failure: they place the control inside model-readable text rather than inside code that physically stops the call.

q: An internal chatbot lets employees query their own HR records through a tool that calls the HR database. Two employees in the same department report that when they ask nearly identical questions, one occasionally sees a fragment of the other's salary data mixed into the response. The engineering team wants to fix the root cause rather than add a warning banner to the chat.
o: Scope every HR-record query to the authenticated identity of the current user at the point the tool executes, rather than trusting the model to filter results in conversation
Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to only discuss the current user's own data
Fine-tune a smaller, cheaper model specifically for the HR chatbot
Log every conversation so leaks can be reviewed after the fact
e: Authorization has to be enforced where the query actually executes, scoped to the authenticated caller, not left to the model's judgment inside the conversation. A system-prompt instruction is advisory and can fail under model error or a crafted request, which is exactly the failure mode already occurring. Model size has no bearing on per-user data scoping. Logging is detective, not preventive; it documents leaks after they've already happened instead of stopping them.

q: A security engineer is auditing a Claude-powered agent's supply chain for integrity risk, even though the model itself has not been altered. The agent connects to three MCP servers pulled fresh from a public registry at every deployment with no version pinning, and its long-running memory file accumulates facts across sessions with no validation step before they're written.
o: Confidentiality failure, because MCP servers pulled from a public registry are inherently exposed
Memory integrity failure, because unvalidated facts can persist into every future session
Availability failure, because an MCP server might go offline during a deployment
Supply-chain integrity failure, because unpinned MCP servers can change behavior between deployments without review
e: The two integrity failure modes actually present are supply-chain integrity (unpinned dependencies pulled fresh each deploy can change agent behavior without any review step) and memory integrity (a persistent memory file that accepts new facts without validation lets a false fact compound forward into every later session). "Public registry" describes where the servers come from, not a confidentiality property of the data the agent handles, so that option mislabels the risk. Nothing in the scenario describes downtime, so availability doesn't apply here even though it's a real property in other contexts.

q: A deployed agent runs for many hours in a single session, taking on new subtasks as they arrive. By the end of the day it stops enforcing a formatting rule it applied correctly during the first two hours, even though nothing has removed that rule from the system prompt. The team wants a fix that addresses the actual failure without discarding conversation history early. Which change addresses it?
o: Increase the model's context window size so more history fits
Restate the durable rule at natural decision points, and start a fresh session at task boundaries instead of running one indefinitely long session
Summarize the entire session so far and replace it with the summary
Move the rule out of the system prompt and repeat it in every user turn instead
e: This is context drift, not bloat: the rule never left the window, it got crowded out by accumulating, competing content. The fix is session hygiene. A bigger window (A) doesn't stop newer content from crowding out the rule, it just delays the symptom. Summarizing the session (C) is compaction, a bloat fix aimed at a capacity problem this stem doesn't describe. Moving the rule out of the stable system layer and into every user turn (D) does the opposite of session hygiene, it makes the durable rule compete with per-request content on every single turn.

q: An agentic pipeline calls a search API that returns full HTML pages and a code-execution tool that returns entire stdout logs. Token spend and latency have grown steadily as the pipeline chains more tool calls per task, even though none of the pipeline's instructions have changed. Which change is most likely to produce the largest reduction in context consumed per task?
o: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the same payloads fit more comfortably
Summarize the conversation history every five turns
Filter and truncate the raw tool outputs to only the fields the next step actually needs, before they enter context
Lower the sampling temperature so responses are shorter
e: Tool output pruning is usually the largest single source of bloat in agentic systems, and the stem points straight at it: growth tracks tool calls, not turn count. A larger window (A) tolerates the waste rather than eliminating it, and cost still scales with it. Summarizing history every five turns (B) is compaction, which targets accumulated turns, not the raw tool payloads the stem identifies as the actual bulk. Temperature (D) affects sampling randomness, not payload size, and isn't a reliable lever on output length.

q: A long-running coding session nears its context limit, so the team enables automatic compaction to summarize and replace older turns whenever the window is 80% full, without specifying what the summary must retain. Two weeks later, an agent forgets a constraint that was established early in a session and never revisited afterward. What is the most accurate explanation?
o: Compaction is non-lossy, so the constraint must have been removed by something else
The context window itself expired, unrelated to compaction
The constraint was never in context because system prompts do not persist across compaction
Compaction discarded the constraint because the summary boundary was left as a default rather than a deliberate design decision about what must survive
e: Compaction is lossy by design, and what survives it has to be a deliberate design decision, usually decisions and outcomes rather than transcript detail. Leaving that undefined means an early, never-repeated constraint is exactly the kind of detail that gets summarized away. Option A is factually wrong, compaction is explicitly lossy. Option B invents a mechanism ('window expiry') that isn't how context management works. Option D describes a real risk, but it is not what happened here since the trap is the missing design decision, not that system prompts categorically fail to survive compaction.

q: A coding agent needs to search a large monorepo to locate every caller of a deprecated function before making a change. The team wants a guarantee that the raw search results, which can run to tens of thousands of tokens per query, never appear in the parent agent's context, only a distilled list of file paths and line numbers. Which design provides that guarantee?
o: Delegate the search to a subagent with its own context window, returning only the condensed result to the parent
Instruct the parent agent's system prompt to 'keep tool results brief and summarized'
Prune the search tool's output to the first 500 tokens before returning it
Increase max_tokens on the parent so it can hold the full result set without truncation
e: Only isolating the search inside a subagent's own context window structurally guarantees the raw results never reach the parent, the parent simply never sees them. A system-prompt instruction (B) is a request the model can still fail to follow, not a guarantee, exactly the gap between a prompt and a deterministic control. Pruning to a fixed length (C) still lets raw, truncated content into the parent's context, violating the 'never appear' requirement, and risks cutting the exact lines the change needs. Raising max_tokens (D) increases capacity for the full result set, the opposite of keeping it out.

q: An extraction pipeline uses output_config.format with a JSON Schema to pull a customer name, account ID, and support tier from a transcript. QA reports zero schema validation failures over the past month. A downstream billing job that trusts the extracted account_id field has been charging the wrong customers. Investigation shows every extracted record was valid JSON matching the schema exactly. What does this reveal?
o: The schema must be malformed, since valid records shouldn't cause wrong charges
Schema validation guarantees shape and type, not that the extracted values are the correct ones; a semantic validation step is still required
output_config.format is unreliable and should be replaced with prompt-only instructions asking for JSON
The billing job should retry the extraction request until it gets a different account_id
e: Schema-valid and semantically correct are different guarantees. The schema confirms shape, types, and required fields; it says nothing about whether account_id actually belongs to the right customer, that requires a separate domain-level check. Nothing in the stem indicates the schema itself is broken (A), a technically valid document is not evidence of a malformed schema. Constrained decoding did its job producing well-formed output (C); reverting to prompt-only JSON requests would remove that structural guarantee without adding the missing semantic check. Retrying the same extraction (D) doesn't fix a systematically wrong mapping and still skips the validation step that was actually missing.

q: A summarization service must never route a partially generated response to a human reviewer for 'cleanup,' because reviewers have started unintentionally inventing plausible-sounding endings for cut-off summaries. The service already sets a generous max_tokens. Which check enforces that 'never' requirement deterministically, rather than depending on a reviewer's judgment each time?
o: A prompt instruction telling the reviewer not to guess when a summary looks incomplete
A style guide asking writers to flag incomplete-looking summaries before editing them
Code that inspects stop_reason and automatically routes anything other than end_turn or stop_sequence away from the reviewer, before it's ever displayed
A larger max_tokens value so truncation becomes rare enough to ignore in practice
e: Checking stop_reason in code and gating on it is a deterministic control the reviewer's compliance can't undermine, exactly the distinction between a request and a guarantee that a 'must never' requirement calls for. A prompt instruction to the reviewer (A) and a style guide (B) both depend on a human noticing and complying every single time, which is precisely the failure already happening. A larger max_tokens value (D) reduces how often truncation occurs but doesn't eliminate it, 'rare enough to ignore' is not the same as never, and max_tokens can still be hit.

q: A team's classification prompt embeds the specific customer email being processed directly inside the system parameter, alongside the durable classification rules and category definitions. After moving to production traffic, every request is billed at full input-token price even though the classification rules and category list never change between calls. What is the most likely cause?
o: The rules and categories are too long to benefit from caching regardless of placement
Per-request content inside the system parameter changes the prefix on every call, which breaks the cache match against the otherwise-stable rules
Classification tasks are ineligible for prompt caching entirely
The category list must be moved into a tool schema before caching can apply
e: Prompt caching matches a stable prefix. Mixing per-request data into system changes that prefix on every call, so the otherwise-durable rules never get a cache hit. Length (A) isn't the disqualifier here, a long stable prefix caches fine on its own. Caching isn't categorically unavailable for classification (C), the technique applies to any stable prefix regardless of task type. Moving content into a tool schema (D) isn't required for caching to work, the fix is separating stable content from per-request content, not migrating the whole prompt into tools.

q: An agent has a single tool named update_record whose description reads only 'updates a record.' The agent's system prompt is thorough but never mentions this tool by name. In testing, the agent calls update_record on read-only requests and supplies malformed arguments roughly a third of the time. Which change is most likely to fix the behavior?
o: Add tool-usage guidance to the system prompt instead of touching the tool's own description
Instruct the user, in their turns, to specify exactly when the tool should be used
Reduce max_tokens so the agent has less room to over-elaborate before calling the tool
Rewrite the tool's description and parameter descriptions with the same clarity given to the system prompt, including when not to call it
e: Tool descriptions are prompts: the model conditions its tool-calling decision directly on that text, so a vague description produces the same ambiguity failure a vague system prompt would, just with worse consequences. Adding guidance elsewhere in the system prompt (A) doesn't fix it, because the failure lives at the specific surface the model reads when deciding to call this tool, not at the surface that already exists and clearly isn't reaching it. Pushing the responsibility onto end users every turn (B) is unreliable and doesn't scale, it substitutes a durable, one-time fix with a per-request one. max_tokens (C) caps output length; it has no bearing on which tool gets called or with what arguments.

q: A prompt update resolves a customer-reported failure where an agent wrongly refused a legitimate refund request. The engineer ships the change the same day, since the reported case now passes and nothing else has been reported. Three weeks later, support tickets show the agent has started approving refund requests it previously correctly declined. What should have happened before shipping?
o: The change should have been verified against the fixed eval set covering both approval and decline cases, not just the reported one
The change should have been reviewed by a second engineer before merge
The change should have shipped with a lower max_tokens value to constrain the response
The change should have been tested only against additional refusal cases, since refusal was the category that originally failed
e: A prompt fix for one case commonly regresses others, which is exactly why the eval set has to run before shipping, not just the reported case. Code review by a second engineer (B) doesn't substitute for behavioral regression testing, a human can approve wording that still fails eval cases neither reviewer thought to check by eye. max_tokens (C) is unrelated to decision correctness. Testing only refusal cases (D) would still miss the regression that surfaced here, which appeared in the approval category, not the one that originally failed.

q: A pipeline must never let instructions embedded inside an uploaded file override its summarization task, regardless of what the file contains. It currently builds its prompt by concatenating the uploaded file's raw text directly into the same string that carries the summarization instructions. Which two changes together enforce that guarantee structurally, rather than relying on the model choosing to ignore embedded instructions? (Select two.)
o: Wrap the uploaded content in a clearly delimited tag, such as <untrusted_document>, before including it
Reject any file whose content contains common trigger words like 'ignore' or 'instructions'
Never interpolate the raw uploaded text directly into the instruction-bearing portion of the prompt; keep it in a clearly separated data section
Increase max_tokens so the model has enough room to safely process longer files
e: Delimiting untrusted content clearly and never interpolating it into the instruction layer are the two structural halves of the same technique, together they stop injected text from sharing a channel with the instructions the application trusts. A keyword blocklist (B) is trivially bypassed by rephrasing and isn't the named mitigation, it's a request-level patch, not a structural one. max_tokens (D) controls output length and has nothing to do with whether embedded text is treated as data or as an instruction.

q: A prompt currently includes one example of correctly formatted output, and real-world outputs are inconsistent in tone and structure. A teammate proposes adding four more examples that are nearly identical to the original, just with different customer names swapped in, arguing that more examples always improve consistency. What is the correct critique of that plan?
o: It's wrong to add more examples at all; one well-placed example is already sufficient, and Claude should never receive more than one
The examples should be moved from the system prompt into a tool description so they load faster

The number of examples isn't the fix here; the added examples aren't diverse, so they risk teaching an incidental pattern rather than the actual format rule; construct examples that vary in ways that matter, not just add volume
The fix is to reduce the model's effort level rather than change the examples
e: Diversity, not raw count, is what makes few-shot examples work, near-identical examples risk teaching an incidental pattern (like the customer-name field) instead of the actual formatting rule this objective is about constructing examples well. Option A asserts a rigid shot-count ceiling as if it were settled fact; how many examples to use is Domain 5's shot-count taxonomy, not a claim this objective makes, and the claim itself is not defensible on its face. Tool descriptions (B) aren't a loading-speed mechanism and don't address the diversity problem. Effort level (D) is an unrelated Domain 5 lever (thinking and reasoning effort) that has no bearing on example construction or output formatting.

q: A team's weather-alerting tool calls an external forecasting API. The tool definition hardcodes the API key as a default value directly inside the tool's input schema so the agent can pass it through automatically, and the same tool definition is deployed unchanged straight from staging into production.
o: Move the API key into the tool's description field so the model can see that it is required
Ask the model to redact the API key from its own responses whenever it appears
Pull the API key from a secret manager at execution time, scoped to the minimum access needed, and treat the endpoint as per-environment configuration rather than a value baked into the schema
Increase the tool's timeout so staging and production behave identically
e: Credentials belong in a secret manager scoped to least privilege, and endpoints belong in per-environment configuration, never embedded in a schema the model reads and that ships unchanged between environments. Putting the key in the description field makes the leak risk worse, since that text is model-readable context that can be echoed back. Asking the model to redact the key is a detective patch on a problem that should never have put a secret in context in the first place. Timeout has nothing to do with credential handling or environment separation.

q: An engineer is designing an agent that runs shell commands on a customer's machine using Anthropic's own Bash tool schema, and separately searches the web using Anthropic's web search tool. She assumes that because both tools come from Anthropic, both are executed on Anthropic's infrastructure and neither requires her own code to run anything.
o: Both assumptions are correct; Anthropic executes any tool whose schema it defines

The Bash tool is a client tool that her own infrastructure must execute and return as a tool_result; web search is a server tool that Anthropic's infrastructure executes and returns as a server_tool_use result
Neither tool requires execution at all; both return results directly from the model's training data
Web search is a client tool she must execute herself, while the Bash tool runs entirely on Anthropic's infrastructure
e: Whether a tool is client-side or server-side depends on who executes it, not who authored the schema. The Bash tool is Anthropic-defined but still a client tool: her own harness has to run the command and return a tool_result. Web search is genuinely server-side; Anthropic's infrastructure executes it internally and surfaces a server_tool_use result with no tool_result required from her. The first option wrongly assumes authorship implies execution. The third ignores that tools by definition act on something outside the model's parameters. The fourth reverses the actual client/server assignment of the two tools named.

q: An agent has both a read-only list_invoices tool and a void_invoice tool that permanently cancels a customer invoice with no undo. The team originally required a human to confirm every single tool call, but within days support staff started reflexively clicking "approve" on every prompt, including for void_invoice.
o: Keep requiring approval on every call, but add a warning icon next to destructive ones
Remove the approval step entirely, since staff aren't reading the prompts anyway
Require two separate staff members to approve every tool call, including read-only ones
Auto-approve read-only calls like list_invoices, and keep an explicit, separate confirmation step only for irreversible actions like void_invoice
e: Approval fatigue happens when every call, regardless of risk, demands identical attention, so oversight collapses into a reflex click; narrowing confirmation to genuinely irreversible actions restores the signal. A warning icon doesn't change the volume of approvals causing the fatigue, and a fatigued reviewer can ignore a visual cue as easily as the prompt itself. Removing approval entirely abandons oversight on the one action that most needs it. Requiring two approvers on every call, including read-only ones, adds friction without addressing why staff stopped reading prompts in the first place, making the fatigue worse.

q: A platform team maintains one shared tool set used by every agent session, including a rarely used purge_tenant_data tool invoked by only two administrators a few times a year. Every session pays the token cost of that tool's full definition on every request regardless of who is logged in, and tool-selection accuracy has been degrading as the shared set has grown.
o: Move purge_tenant_data out of the default set and load it only into the small number of sessions run by the administrators who actually need it
Shorten the tool's name to reduce its token count
Add a longer, more detailed description to purge_tenant_data so the model understands it better
Convert purge_tenant_data into an MCP server so it no longer counts against the context window
e: Every registered tool definition is sent on every request whether or not it's used, and a larger shared set also increases selection ambiguity; scoping a rarely needed, high-privilege tool to only the sessions that need it removes both costs at once. Shortening the name saves a negligible number of tokens and does nothing about ambiguity. A longer description makes the per-request token cost worse without addressing who needs the tool. Moving the tool to MCP is a common misconception: MCP tool definitions are still declared to the model on every request and still consume context tokens, so this doesn't exempt it from the cost described.

q: A team is building an agent that needs to run Python snippets to validate calculations before presenting results to users. An engineer starts drafting a custom tool schema that shells out to a sandboxed Python interpreter that their infrastructure team would need to build and maintain going forward.
o: Use Anthropic's built-in code execution tool instead, since the capability already exists and doesn't need to be rebuilt
Build the custom tool as planned, since custom tools are always more secure than built-in ones
Write a Skill that teaches Claude to simulate Python execution by reasoning through the code manually
Package the custom sandbox as an MCP server so it can be reused later
e: The first question in the decision framework is whether the capability already exists as an Anthropic-provided tool. It does here, so building and maintaining a parallel sandbox is wasted effort with no capability gained. The claim that custom tools are inherently more secure than built-in ones is simply false; built-in tools are Anthropic-maintained and don't automatically lose on security. A Skill can't substitute for a missing execution capability — no amount of procedural guidance lets Claude actually run code without a real execution environment. Wrapping the redundant sandbox as an MCP server still rebuilds a capability that already exists, plus adds infrastructure ownership on top.

q: A support team wants every response from their Claude-powered agent to follow a specific tone, always cite the relevant help-center article, and always close with a specific escalation phrase. The agent can already read the help-center article library and compose responses; nothing about its capabilities is missing.
o: A custom tool that formats and returns the final response text
An MCP server exposing a format_response endpoint
A Skill containing the tone rules, citation convention, and closing phrase
A built-in tool configured with the escalation phrase as a parameter
e: Nothing here is a missing capability — the agent can already read articles and write responses — so the need is entirely about how it should perform a task it can already do, which is exactly what a Skill is for. A custom tool and an MCP server both reach for infrastructure that adds a capability the agent doesn't lack; wrapping 'write it this way' logic in a tool call adds integration overhead for a purely instructional need. There is no generic built-in tool for a company-specific tone and escalation phrase, so that option is fabricated.

q: A platform group runs a single internal API that checks employee time-off balances. Right now only the HR onboarding agent calls it, the API changes only when the onboarding agent's own team changes it, and there are no plans to expose it to any other application.
o: An MCP server maintained independently of the onboarding agent
A custom tool defined directly inside the onboarding agent's application
A Skill describing how to interpret time-off balances
Anthropic's built-in tool for HR systems
e: The deciding question is reuse across applications plus independent maintenance, and neither is true here: one app, one owning team, no separate lifecycle. A custom tool defined in that app is the simplest fit with no unneeded infrastructure. Standing up a separate MCP server buys nothing when there is only one caller and one team maintaining it in lockstep with the app. Checking a balance is a capability the agent doesn't currently have — calling an API — not a procedural or instructional need, so a Skill doesn't fit. There is no generic Anthropic-provided HR tool; that option should be recognized as invented.

q: An engineering-assistant agent needs to periodically spin off a focused code-security review that reads an entire large repository, large enough that pulling all of it into the main conversation would crowd out everything else the user is discussing. The security review also needs read-only filesystem access that the main conversation must never be granted.
o: A Skill containing the security review checklist, loaded into the main conversation
A custom tool that returns the entire repository as text
An MCP server that exposes the repository as a resource
A subagent with its own context window and its own, narrower tool permissions
e: Two needs are described: a separate context window so the large read doesn't crowd out the main conversation, and different, narrower tool permissions than the main conversation should have. Both point to a subagent, which gets its own context and its own scoped access. A Skill loads into the current conversation and inherits its existing permissions, so it solves neither problem. A custom tool that dumps the whole repository as text puts the crowding problem straight into context instead of isolating it. An MCP server can supply read access to the data but doesn't address context isolation or permission scoping on its own.

q: A team wants their support agent to always summarize tickets using the company's specific five-section format, something the agent can already do by writing text, and separately to look up real-time shipment tracking from a carrier's API, which the agent currently has no way to access. Several other product teams beyond support already want shipment tracking, and the carrier integration will be versioned and patched independently by a platform team.
o: A custom tool for the five-section format, and a Skill for shipment tracking
A Skill for the five-section format, and an MCP server for the shipment-tracking capability
A single MCP server that handles both the formatting and the tracking lookup
A built-in tool for the five-section format, and a custom tool for shipment tracking
e: The two needs split cleanly: the five-section format is purely instructional, since the agent already has the capability to write text and just needs a convention, which is a Skill; shipment tracking is a missing capability, reused across multiple teams and independently versioned by a platform team, which is exactly the reuse-plus-independent-maintenance combination that points to an MCP server. Reversing the two is wrong on both counts: a tool for pure formatting is unnecessary machinery, and a Skill cannot grant the actual capability to call a carrier API. Bundling both into one MCP server puts an instructional need into infrastructure it doesn't need. There is no generic built-in tool for a company-specific format, and a bare custom tool ignores that the tracking capability is reused and independently maintained.
